doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Integration and the death of the Negro League and school music programs
summary: Stewart reflects that integration ended the Negro League and led southern schools to cancel music and phys ed programs.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I see. Well did you have an inkling when you were nine or ten that you would be in music as a living?

No. I had no idea. I had no idea. I started playing — when I was nine or ten I was still — at eight years old I was still in New York. And the reason we saw so many different cities — New York and Philadelphia and Newport, Rhode Island and then back to New York in 1968 — was because I lived with my grandparents. My father was still kind of playing ball by the early fifties and he just retired, kind of by that time the Negro League kind of phased out. And there was no hurrah at the end of it for him.

Oh that’s too bad. You know someone made a point, I had never thought about it, when Jackie Robinson joined the pros that that was a very important thing and good for him and all that, but it meant the death —

It was the kiss of death of the Negro League for sure. I mean a lot of things happened like I don’t want to get too far off the subject but if you think about integration I mean it was © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

a great thing while at the same time it was almost like you led people down this garden path following this carrot until you finally caught them. Because one of the byproducts of integration was they canceled the music programs and the phys ed programs in a lot of schools in the south and said they had to pay for the busing so they didn’t have any music and art.

Right. My father was in Shreveport, Louisiana and they basically canceled the music program and they were about to cancel the phys ed program and some kind of way they finagled it so they didn’t. But a lot of programs got canceled like that.
In the public schools because they said all right you’ve made us do this—
Right, so now you have to pay for the busing and we’ll cancel the two things that you may excel in at that time.
